cues.text: A nickname from Dad
Alessandro Rosa Vieira grew up in the north of São Paulo, Brazil.
His father, João, was a butcher who also played football on neighbourhood fields.
People there called João "Falcão", and his son was given the same nickname.
At twelve, the boy joined Guapira, a small futsal club near home.
As a teenager at Corinthians, he tried the big grass game again and again.
Seven times he spent two or three months playing on grass, and seven times he came back to futsal, the small indoor game that was his true love.
Not every path fits the first time. It is okay to go back to what you love.
Doors that stayed shut
For a few years, Falcão changed teams again and again.
In 2001, a big football club called Palmeiras gave him a trial on grass.
He scored, and people praised his play, but the club only asked for more time and never gave him a clear answer.
So he went back to his futsal team.
In 2002 he tried another club, Portuguesa, and again it did not work out.
Knock on the three paper doors.
Two stay shut.
The third opens in 2003, at Jaraguá, the futsal team where he finally settled.
A no is not the end of your story. Keep knocking, and another door can open.
A dream for Dad
Early in 2004, Falcão's father died.
His dad had always dreamed of seeing his son play football on a big grass pitch.
That same year Falcão was named the best futsal player in the world, but many people would still feel a deep sadness after losing a parent.
In 2005, the São Paulo football club signed him to play on grass.
His first game came exactly one year after his father died.
He played thirteen games in about six months, then turned back to futsal.
Trying something for someone you love is brave, even when it does not last.
It is okay to feel sad and to talk about someone you miss. Their love goes with you.
So close, again and again
Falcão's first World Cup was in 2000, when he was twenty-three.
Brazil reached the final but lost to Spain, four goals to three.
In 2004 he was named the best player of the tournament, yet Brazil finished third.
The wait for a world title went on.
In 2008, the World Cup came to Brazil.
Falcão said that if they lost again, it would be hard to wear the Brazil shirt again.
Flip the scoreboard.
This time Brazil were champions at home, and he was the best player of the tournament once more.
You are more than one result. A loss can be the start of trying again.
Hurt, but not alone
Just days before the 2012 World Cup in Thailand, Falcão hurt his left calf and was nearly left out of the team.
The coaches insisted he stay with the group and have intensive treatment.
The stress even made part of his face stop moving for a while.
He played only thirty-seven minutes in the whole tournament.
In the final, Brazil were losing to Spain with three minutes left, when Falcão scored to make it level.
Score the equaliser, then watch his teammate Neto win it in extra time, three goals to two.
When you are hurt, let other people help you. A team can carry you through.
One last World Cup
After 2012, Falcão said that World Cup had been his last, but he changed his mind.
At thirty-nine, he prepared all year for one more.
In Colombia he scored ten goals and became the top scorer in World Cup history, with forty-eight.
Then Brazil played Iran and drew, four goals each.
Falcão scored three, and his penalty too, but Brazil lost the shootout and were knocked out.
Lift the paper players.
The Iran team raised Falcão into the air to honour him, and he cried.
A sad ending can still be full of respect.
Setbacks and new paths are part of every great story. You are more than one result.
